summary:
Mission Moon is a Roblox spaceflight game in which players design, fund and fly an Earth-to-Moon mission. They build a rocket from 15 NASA-style parts (boosters, fuel tanks and crew vehicles) on a $2 billion budget. The ship needs enough range to reach the Moon, and 48 of the 80 possible builds can do it. Players then launch, fly a cockpit sequence, land and explore on a limited oxygen supply. On the Moon they inspect five Apollo-era instruments, find a wrecked pod, collect Moon stones with a handheld detector and radio their findings to NASA. They finish by re-entering and splashing down.

The game turns hard-to-picture space engineering into choices. Players see the real scale of rockets, feel the cost limits and weigh fuel against power. The data comes from public NASA sources, including the NASA Inspector General’s cost report and “Stages to Saturn.” This matters because people remember what they do better than what they read. A game lets anyone learn why space missions are expensive, difficult and worth the effort.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Moon is a Roblox game that takes a player through a whole Earth-to-Moon mission.

  1. Design and budget: The player builds a rocket from 15 NASA-style parts: 5 boosters, 5 fuel tanks and 5 crew vehicles. Everything is paid for from a $2 billion budget. A ship’s range is its fuel capacity times its booster efficiency, plus a bonus from the crew vehicle, and it needs a range of 80 to reach the Moon. Of the 80 possible builds, 48 make it on this budget.
  2. Launch: Countdown, stage separation and a first-person cockpit sequence. For tall rockets the camera zooms out so the whole build stays in view.
  3. Moon: The player has 4 minutes of oxygen and wears a NASA-style space suit. They inspect five Apollo-era instruments, each with a fact card, and find a wrecked pod. After the fifth inspection, NASA radios in and three Moon stones appear. A handheld detector shows how far away the nearest stone is.
  4. Return: Launch home, re-entry with heating effects, parachutes and splashdown. Missions earn extra funding, which pays for a bigger rocket next time.

Benefits

  • It shows the real size of launch vehicles.
  • It makes cost visible, so players learn why missions are expensive.
  • It lets players try engineering trade-offs and fail safely.
  • It teaches what Apollo left on the Moon.
  • Anyone with a Roblox account can play it, with nothing to install beyond Roblox.

Intended impact
We want players, especially students, to leave with a feel for how hard and costly space exploration is. Seeing the numbers as choices makes them easier to remember than reading them.

Tools and technology

  • Roblox Studio, with all game logic in Luau.
  • Server scripts and ModuleScripts for the game state, ship building, space suit and launch complex.
  • Client LocalScripts for flight, re-entry, the detector HUD and the inspect highlights.
  • Roblox’s built-in lighting, atmosphere, particle, trail and bloom systems for the visual effects.
  • Claude (Anthropic’s AI) helped write and test the code and built the 3D models through Studio’s tools.
  • A Slides deck for the presentation.
  • No special hardware: a normal computer running Roblox Studio.

Data
We used public NASA material:

  • The NASA Inspector General report IG-22-003 for per-launch costs.
  • NASA History’s “Stages to Saturn” (SP-4206) for Saturn V design.
  • NASA fact sheets for SLS and Orion.
  • Apollo mission records for the instruments.

What is creative about it

  • It turns an audit report’s numbers into a build-and-fly game.
  • It has a full mission arc: design, launch, explore, collect, return.
  • It has hands-on touches such as the stone detector, the space suit, heated metal and plasma effects on re-entry, and detailed models of the real instruments.
  • Funding earned in one mission feeds the next, so success changes what you can build.

What we considered

  • Accuracy vs. fun: Part prices are scaled estimates, and the range of 80 is a game rule, not real orbital mechanics. We say so openly.
  • Balance: The budget allows many builds but not all, so choices matter and failure is possible.
  • Clarity: Fact cards show their source, and the inspect prompt disappears after one use so players don’t repeat themselves.
  • Comfort and readability: Re-entry effects were toned down so they aren’t too bright, and the launch camera adjusts for tall rockets.
  • Playtime: A mission fits in a few minutes.
dataRefs: NASA OIG Report IG-22-003: NASA’s Readiness for the Artemis Missions (SLS, Orion and ground systems cost per launch)
NASA History SP-4206: Stages to Saturn (Saturn V stage design and sizes)
